study.title: A Quantum Lower Bound for Triangle Finding

cover.headline: **Quantum computers may have a harder limit** on finding patterns in networks than researchers hoped.

slides.title: If this holds, some network problems might stay out of reach even with quantum speedup.
slides.body:
Quantum computers promise to search certain structures faster than ordinary machines. But this early paper suggests a floor.

That could mean some pattern-detection tasks will always be expensive, even in a quantum future.

slides.title: The team reports that finding triangles in a network requires at least N to the power 13/12 queries.
slides.body:
For graphs with N vertices, the best quantum algorithms use about N to the power 5/4 queries. The new lower bound is N to the power 13/12.

That narrows the gap between possible and necessary.

slides.title: Triangle finding means detecting when three nodes in a graph all connect to each other.
slides.body:
It is a benchmark problem in quantum algorithm design. For years, the lower bound was just N queries, the cost of unstructured search.

The work compares graphs with a planted triangle to random triangle-free graphs.

caveats: This is a preprint. It has not been peer reviewed yet, so no independent expert has checked the work.
The implication slide reflects our interpretation. The paper itself establishes a mathematical lower bound, not a claim about future quantum hardware.

source.abstract: Triangle finding is a fundamental problem in graph theory that has played a central role in the development of quantum algorithmic techniques. For $N$-vertex graphs given by their adjacency matrices, a long line of work has improved the quantum query upper bound from $O(N^{3/2})$ to $O(N^{5/4})$. However, the best known lower bound has remained the elementary $Ω(N)$ bound obtained from unstructured search. We prove the first superlinear quantum query lower bound for triangle finding, showing that $Ω(N^{13/12})$ queries are necessary. Our result also implies the same lower bound for triangle detection and for detecting every fixed connected non-bipartite graph. The proof builds on the compressed oracle approach of Zhandry and the transfer approaches of Belovs. It compares the computation on graphs with a planted triangle to the computation on random graphs conditioned to be triangle-free, through a map on the input registers that almost commutes with every query. We average over local changes to the input while preserving its distribution, through a procedure known as conditional resampling. Our main technical contribution is a set of estimates that let us control the query error under this averaging, despite the dependence introduced by conditioning a dense graph to be triangle-free.
